analysis.one_liner: Charges fossil fuel producers a rising per-ton emissions fee and sends most of the money back as monthly household rebates.
analysis.headline: The carbon fee-and-dividend bill was sent to 10 House committees, never got a hearing or a vote, and expired when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have charged oil, gas, and coal producers and importers a fee for every ton of greenhouse gases their fuels emit, starting at $15 per ton in 2020 and rising each year. About 70% of the money would go back to households as a monthly dividend that phases out for incomes above $80,000 (single) or $130,000 (married), with the rest funding infrastructure, clean-energy research, and help for workers and towns that depend on fossil fuel jobs. It also would have charged a fee on imports from countries without carbon pricing so U.S. manufacturers were not undercut.
analysis.who_benefits: Low- and middle-income households would receive a monthly cash dividend funded by the fee — most energy costs fall hardest on lower incomes, so a flat per-person rebate with a phaseout above roughly $80,000–$130,000 would leave most working households better off. Fossil fuel workers would get wage insurance, retraining, relocation help, and pension and health benefits protection, including the United Mine Workers pension plan. Communities dependent on fossil fuels, rural and low-income areas facing higher energy bills, and farmers paid for carbon-storing practices would also get dedicated funding. Everyone would benefit from cleaner air and from infrastructure spending — roads, transit, water systems, rural broadband — that must pay prevailing wages and use American-made materials.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low- and middle-income households and fossil fuel workers

how_it_helps.text: Sends 70% of carbon fee revenue to households as a monthly dividend — one full share per adult, half per child — that cannot be counted against eligibility for any other federal benefit program.
Targets the money at ordinary incomes: the dividend phases out only above $80,000 for single filers and $130,000 for joint filers, and is reduced 5% per $1,000 over the threshold.

Funds transition help for workers displaced by the fees, modeled on trade adjustment assistance: wage insurance, relocation expenses, early retirement, retraining, and pension and health benefits including the 1974 UMWA miners' pension plan; plus energy bill aid (LIHEAP) and community economic development grants.

Spends 20% of revenue on infrastructure — highways, mass transit, passenger rail, drinking water, rural broadband, Superfund and mine reclamation — with all projects required to pay prevailing (Davis-Bacon) wages and use American-made iron, steel, cement, and manufactured goods.
Sets emissions targets of 45% below 2017 levels by 2030 and roughly 90% below by 2050, and escalates the fee faster (+$30/year instead of +$15) whenever the country misses a yearly target.
Pays farmers and landowners for carbon-sequestering practices like cover crops, no-till farming, reforestation, and wetland restoration, and funds direct air capture and carbon capture refunds.

Charges a border fee on carbon-intensive imports from countries without comparable carbon pricing and refunds U.S. exporters, protecting domestic manufacturers from being undercut by pollution from abroad.

analysis.who_pays: Oil, gas, and coal producers and importers would pay the fee, which they would pass along in fuel prices — that is the point, to make pollution reflect its cost. Households above the dividend phaseout thresholds ($80,000 single / $130,000 joint) would pay higher energy prices with no rebate. Energy-intensive manufacturers (steel, cement, aluminum, chemicals, glass) would face higher fuel costs, though the border adjustment shields them from dirtier foreign competition. Drivers in rural areas with long commutes would see the largest price increases relative to their rebates.
analysis.who_pays_short: Fossil fuel producers and higher-income households

drawbacks.text: Energy prices rise immediately and the fee climbs $15 every year — and by $30 a year if emissions targets are missed — so the cost of gasoline, heating oil, natural gas, and electricity would grow substantially through the 2020s, with the first dividends starting roughly nine months after enactment (though an advance payment was due the month before the first fee collection).

The dividend is taxable income, and the phaseout is a steep cliff: a two-earner household crossing $130,000 in income loses the whole family's rebate within a few thousand dollars, creating a sharp effective tax increase for upper-middle-income families.

Only 70% of revenue is rebated to people; 30% goes to federal infrastructure, research, and transition programs, so some households — particularly high-mileage rural drivers and households above the income thresholds — would pay more in higher energy prices than they get back.

Hitting the schedule would require cutting covered-fuel emissions to 45% of 2017 levels by 2030, an unusually fast pace that would force rapid changes in how Americans heat homes, generate power, and travel, with real disruption costs concentrated in coal, oil, and gas regions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For most working households the design is protective: the monthly dividend is meant to more than cover the average family's higher energy bills, and the phaseout concentrates the benefit below $80,000–$130,000 of income. The honest costs are real — energy prices climb steadily from day one, the transition is fast, the income phaseout creates a punishing cliff, and 30% of the money funds programs instead of going back to people. On balance it was a deliberately progressive carbon tax that shifted costs to fossil fuel producers and higher earners, but it was never tested by a single hearing, so none of these trade-offs were ever debated on the record.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to ten House committees when introduced, got nothing but subcommittee referrals, and died quietly when the term ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jimmy Panetta introduced the bill on July 25, 2019, joined by Rep. Thomas Suozzi; it received five cosponsors, all Democrats.

At introduction it was referred to ten committees at once — Ways and Means plus nine others — a structure that splits a bill into pieces and requires many committees to act before the full House can vote.
The only further actions were referrals to subcommittees in July and August 2019; the last action of any kind was a subcommittee referral on August 14, 2019.
No committee ever held a hearing, marked the bill up, or reported it, and no floor vote ever occurred; the bill expired when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil fuel producers and importers came out ahead — they never faced the fee, which would have started at $15 per ton and risen every year. Higher-income households also came out ahead, since they would have paid higher energy prices with no rebate.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no roll-call exists; all six House supporters were Democrats and no Republican cosponsored, but there is no record of who actively opposed it.

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers and refiners
industries.note: Refiners, gas producers, and importers would pay the fee on every ton their fuels emit, starting at $15 in 2020 and rising $15 each year — the mechanism designed to shrink their market over time. Their interest in blocking the bill ran against the public benefit the fee was meant to fund.

Coal producers and importers face the same per-ton fee, which rises fastest in effect for the most carbon-intensive fuels; the bill's emissions schedule implies near-elimination of covered emissions by 2050. It did include dedicated funds for miners' pensions and coal-community redevelopment.

industries.industry: Energy-intensive manufacturers (steel, cement, aluminum, chemicals, glass, paper)
industries.note: They would pay the carbon fee through fuel costs, but the border adjustment charges comparable fees on imports from countries without carbon pricing and refunds U.S. exporters, shielding them from being undercut by dirtier foreign production.

industries.industry: Fluorinated gas (refrigerant and industrial chemical) makers
industries.note: A separate fee at 20% of the carbon rate would be imposed on fluorinated greenhouse gases, which are among the most potent heat-trapping gases and a close cousin of the refrigerant phase-down the public already supports.

20% of revenue flows to highways, transit, rail, water, broadband, and weatherization programs, all required to pay prevailing wages and use American-made materials, and 5% funds clean-energy research, storage, grid modernization, and EV charging. Workers in these industries would be the ones hired.
The bill directs payments to farmers and landowners for cover crops, no-till, reforestation, and wetland restoration that store carbon, with third-party verification.
